abstract: Guillain–Barré syndrome (GBS) is an aggressively advancing rapidly autoimmune disorder often triggered by a recent infection that attacks the peripheral nerves, ultimately leading to diminished reflexes, sensory abnormalities, and muscle weakness. Albuminocytological dissociation (ACD), defined as a cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) evaluation depicting normal white blood cell counts, but high protein levels are considered as a pathognomonic feature in the diagnosis of GBS. While ACD has been well-reported in the available literature, its exact cause and etiology remain uncertain; however, some hypothesis suggests inflammation, disrupted nerve barrier function, and altered CSF flow contributes to the pathogenesis of ACD. In this narrative review, we aim to assess its diagnostic value, a viable source in predicting disease severity and evaluate the pathophysiological association between ACD and GBS. We also highlight recent advancements in CSF biomarker research and proteomics that could refine and further improve the diagnosis and treatment of GBS. By consolidating existing knowledge, this review seeks to improve clinical awareness of ACD, guide future investigations, and contribute to better patient management strategies.
body:
Introduction
This article is compliant with the TITAN Guidelines 2025 – governing declaration and use of artificial intelligence
[
1
]
. Guillain–Barré syndrome (GBS) is a rare acute inflammatory disease of peripheral nerves and nerve roots that usually occurs as a postinfective immune-mediated phenomenon. The disease manifests as ascending muscle weakness that starts from the lower extremities and moves to the upper extremities, hyporeflexia, and possible but less prominent sensory symptoms. GBS is the most common form of neuromuscular paralysis in developed countries
[
2
]
. Since the near-elimination of poliomyelitis throughout the world, GBS ranks as the most frequent cause of acute flaccid paralysis, the annual incidence being one or two cases per 100 000 population
[
3
]
. GBS usually follows a gastrointestinal or upper respiratory infection. It has been associated with
Campylobacter jejuni
, Mycoplasmapneumonia, varicella-zoster virus, cytomegalovirus (CMV), Epstein–Barr virus, HIV, or even COVID-19 infections
[
4
]
.
HIGHLIGHTS
GBS is an acute, immune-mediated polyradiculoneuropathy,
commonly triggered by infections like Campylobacter jejuni, leading to rapidly progressive limb weakness and areflexia.
Molecular mimicry plays a critical role
in the pathogenesis, where antibodies against infectious agents mistakenly attack peripheral nerve components.
Electrodiagnostic studies and cerebrospinal fluid analysis
are essential for confirming GBS, with typical findings including albuminocytologic dissociation in CSF.
Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg) and plasma exchange (PE)
are the main treatments, significantly improving outcomes if started early.
Despite effective treatment, recovery can be prolonged,
and some patients may experience residual deficits, emphasizing the need for long-term rehabilitation and monitoring.
Patients usually present within 1 week to 10 days after the onset of viral infection. Symptoms vary from mild weakness in the lower extremities to complete paralysis of respiratory, bulbar, and facial muscles
[
5
]
. GBS is characterized by rapidly evolving ascending weakness, mild sensory loss, and hyporeflexia or areflexia, progressing to a nadir over up to 4 weeks
[
6
]
. In the initial stages of the syndrome, the patient presents with difficulty in ambulation. However, as the syndrome progresses, profound weakness of hip flexors and knee extensors is also encountered by the patient, making unassisted ambulation impossible
[
7
]
. Severe respiratory muscle weakness necessitating ventilatory support develops in 10–30%
[
8
]
.
The term “albuminocytological dissociation” (ACD) was first coined by Sicard and Foix in 1912 to describe the unexpected finding of elevated cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) protein without pleocytosis in patients with spinal compression
[
9
]
. ACD is defined as an increased total protein (TP) concentration with a normal total nucleated cell count (TNCC). The exact pathophysiology of ACD is unknown, but different mechanisms have been proposed, including the intrathecal production of specific proteins [immunoglobulin G (IgG) and myelin basic protein], dysfunction of the blood–brain barrier, dysfunction of the blood–nerve barrier, decreased CSF flow, and sequestration of CSF in spinal cord compression
[
10
]
. In human medicine, several conditions have been traditionally associated with ACD including infectious and noninfectious meningoencephalitis, intra- and extra-axial tumors, inflammatory polyneuropathy, hydrocephalus, angiitis of the CNS, cerebral venous sinus occlusion, optic nerve disease, facial neuritis, posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome, structural spinal disorders, nervous system toxic exposure, dementia, epileptic seizures, strokes, intrathecal chemotherapy, and subarachnoid hemorrhage
[
11
]
.
ACD has been described in various forms of the GBS spectrum, such as axonal motor or motor-sensory forms [acute motor axonal neuropathy (AMAN), acute motor sensory axonal neuropathy (AMSAN)], the anti-GQ1b spectrum of Miller Fisher syndrome (MFS), and Bickerstaff brainstem encephalitis (BBE). Cytokines, chemokines, antibodies, complement components, and molecules with a putative neuroprotective role or indicating axonal damage have also been examined using different methods. Besides these potential approaches, proteomics has been recently applied to discover potential biomarkers. The overall result of studies supports the immunopathogenesis of GBS, but ACD remained the only consistent CSF biomarker supporting the diagnosis of GBS. Chronic inflammatory neuropathies comprise a heterogeneous group of diseases. Increased protein in the CSF is a supportive factor of chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy, especially in the absence of definite electrophysiologic criteria. A number of other markers have also been investigated in the CSF of patients with chronic inflammatory neuropathies, similar to GBS. However, none have been used in supporting diagnosis, differentiating among syndromes, or predicting the clinical course and treatment responses
[
12
]
.
GBS is a rare acute inflammatory disease of peripheral nerves and nerve roots that usually occurs as a postinfective immune-mediated phenomenon. The disease manifests as ascending muscle weakness that starts from the lower extremities and moves to the upper extremities, hyporeflexia, and possible but less prominent sensory symptoms. ACD is a key diagnostic feature of GBS. ACD is defined as an increased TP concentration with a normal TNCC. This dissociation is an important characteristic of GBS, which is often used in conjunction with a number of medical findings to determine the disease. GBS is distinguished from other neurological disorders by the presence of ACD in the CSF. In order to accurately diagnose and treat patients with GBS, it is essential that healthcare professionals understand this dissociation. The diagnosis of GBS requires a knowledge of ACD
[
12
]
.
The purpose of this narrative review is to explore the relationship between GBS, and ACD. Through a comprehensive analysis of existing literature, this review aims to elucidate the clinical significance of ACD in GBS, its potential as a diagnostic and prognostic marker, and the underlying pathophysiological mechanisms driving this phenomenon. By synthesizing current knowledge and identifying areas for future research, this review seeks to enhance our understanding of GBS and ACD, ultimately informing strategies for improved patient outcomes
[
12
]
.
Pathophysiology of GBS
GBS is an acute inflammatory immune-mediated polyradiculoneuropathy presenting typically with tingling, progressive weakness, autonomic dysfunction, and pain
[
13
,
14
]
. Besides classic presentation of GBS, clinical variants are based on the types of nerve fibers involved (motor, sensory, sensory and motor, cranial or autonomic), predominant mode of fiber injury (demyelinating versus axonal), and the presence of alteration in consciousness
[
6
].
The most common variants of GBS are acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (AIDP), AMAN, and AMSAN. Other rare variants of GBS include MFS, paraparetic GBS, pharyngeal-cervical-brachial weakness, bilateral facial palsy (BFP) with paresthesia, BBE
[
15
,
16
]
(Table
1
)
[
6
,
17
–
20
]
.

GBS can either be infectious or autoimmune. Patients with GBS related to infections frequently produce antibodies against peripheral nerve gangliosides through molecular mimicry
[
20
]
. A bacterial cross-reactive antigen recognized by macrophages and T cells induces B cells to produce an antiganglioside response, which penetrates blood–nerve barrier and activates complement. These antibodies bind both to gangliosides from nerves and to antigens from microbes. Activated endoneurial macrophages release cytokines and free radicals, invade compact myelin, periaxonal space, and block nerve conduction or cause axonal degeneration. Furthermore, activated T cells release proinflammatory cytokines, fix complement, damage Schwann cells, and ultimately produce dissolution of myelin
[
20
]
. To establish that GBS has an autoimmune etiology, Witebsky–Rose postulates
[
21
]
were addressed by Shoenfeld
et al
[
22
]
: (1) autoantigens were demonstrated; (2) the presence of autoantibodies was confirmed; (3) active immunization with myelin constituents was shown to cause an autoimmune phenomenon resembling GBS; and (4) an adoptive transfer of autoantibodies and autoreactive T cells resulted in nerve demyelination, clinical signs, and laboratory findings of GBS
[
23
]
. Additionally, GBS is also commonly seen in association with other autoimmune diseases, changes in T cell subclasses, and changes in cytokine profile
[
20
]
. Willison studied the motor nerve terminal as a model site of injury, and through combined active and passive immunization paradigms, has proven “a neuropathogenic role for murine antiganglioside antibodies and human GBS-associated antisera”
[
24
]
.
GBS is self-limiting, muscle weakness usually reaching its nadir within 2–3 weeks, with partial or complete recovery occurring over weeks to months. The rate of recovery is facilitated by plasma exchange, and its therapeutic effect presumably is related to the removal of circulating factors. Plasma concentrations of cytokines are raised in patients with GBS during the acute phase, but because their circulating half-lives are only a few hours, the effect of plasma exchange on their plasma levels would be short. Complement depletion also is brief. The respective half-lives of IgM and IgA are 5 and 6 days. By contrast, the half-life of IgG – except for the IgG3 subclass (7 days) – is 21 days, much longer than that of the other plasma proteins. The plasma IgG concentration may remain decreased for up to 5 weeks after plasma exchange therapy. Immunopathological studies suggest that the target of immune attack differs with the GBS subtype. In AIDP, the attack appears to be directed against a component of Schwann cells. In AMAN, the attack appears to be against the axolemma and nodes of Ranvier
[
25
]
. These findings indicate that the presence of IgG, which binds effectively with complements and macrophages, is the most important factor in the development of GBS
[
26
]
. A study suggested that the patients who developed AMAN subsequent to
C. jejuni
enteritis had high anti-GM1 IgG antibody titers during the acute phase of the illness
[
27
]
.
Walsh
et al
reported that patients with GBS had anti-GM1 antibodies and that the predominant immunoglobulin class was IgG not IgM. A correlation was found between the presence of these antibodies and the prognosis in terms of disability 3 and 12 months after presentation
[
28
]
. Some previous studies reported various proportions of IgM class antibody alone, but a significant correlation has been shown between electrodiagnosis and anti-GM1 IgG, rather than IgM, antibody
[
29
]
. Kusunoki
et al
found antibody to the minor monosialosylganglioside GM1b to be a useful diagnostic marker of GBS
[
30
]
. The patients with anti-GM1b antibodies have a clinical pattern distinct from that of the other patients with GBS, more frequently showing serological evidence of recent infection by
C. jejuni
. Patients who were anti-GM1b-positive were distinguished by more rapidly progressive, more severe, and predominantly distal weakness. Cranial nerve involvement and sensory deficits were less common in the patients with anti-GM1b antibodies, and the presence of these antibodies was associated with slower recovery. Clinical manifestations predominantly were associated with anti-GM1b antibodies of the IgG isotype
[
31
]
. Anti-GD1a IgG antibody was detected in patients with severe axonal GBS during the acute phase
[
31
]
. Overall, clinical manifestation of GBS subtypes can be seen in Figure
1
.
Figure 1.
Clinical manifestations of GBS subtypes.
Molecular mimicry associated with
C. jejuni
Molecular mimicry is one mechanism by which infectious agents may trigger an immune response against autoantigens. Many reports have presented findings consistent with the mimicry hypothesis, but none have convincingly demonstrated that mimicry is an important mechanism in the development of autoimmune disease
[
31
]
.
Ang
et al
confirmed the role of molecular mimicry in the induction of anti-GM1 IgG antibody in GBS
[
32
]
. The presence of anti-GM1 antibody has been shown to be significantly associated with preceding
C. jejuni
infection. There are numerous reports of patients who developed GBS after receiving bovine brain ganglioside, indicative that an antecedent infectious agent with a ganglioside-like structure causes this syndrome. A lipopolysaccharide (LPS) was extracted from the
C. jejuni
isolated from a patient with GBS who had anti-GM1 IgG antibody
[
33
]
. It reacted with cholera toxin a specific ligand for the GM1-oligosaccharide. Gas–liquid chromatography-mass spectrometric analysis showed that the purified LPS has galactose (Gal),
N
-acetylgalactosamine (GalNAc), and
N
-acetylneuraminic acid – i.e., the sugar components of the GM1 ganglioside. 1
H
nuclear magnetic resonance showed that the oligosaccharide structure protrudes from the LPS core. This terminal structure is identical to that of the terminal tetrasaccharide of the GM1 ganglioside. Other studies established the oligosaccharide structures of GM1-like, GD3-like, and GT1a-like LPSs in three
C. jejuni
strains isolated from patients with GBS
[
34
,
35
]
. The IgG subclass distribution of anti-GM1 antibodies in GBS and GBS-like LPS is limited mainly to IgG1 and IgG3
[
36
]
. Since subclasses IgG1 and IgG3 are characteristic of a T cell-dependent antibody response, helper T cells may be associated with the B-cell production of IgG antibody to the GM1-like LPS in patients with GBS subsequent to
C. jejuni
enteritis
[
25
]
.
Rabbits sensitized with a bovine brain ganglioside mixture containing GM1, GD1a, GD1b, and GT1b developed high anti-GM1 IgG antibody titers and flaccid limb weakness of acute onset; moreover, they had a monophasic illness course
[
36
]
. A pathological investigation of their peripheral nerves showed predominant Wallerian-like degeneration with neither lymphocytic infiltration nor demyelination. IgG was deposited on anterior root axons, and GM1 was present on peripheral nerve axons. Sensitization with purified GM1 also induced axonal neuropathy, indicating that GM1 was the immunogen in the mixture. Inoculation with GM1 may induce high anti-GM1 IgG antibody titers, the autoantibody thereafter binding to the GM1 expressed on rabbit peripheral nerve axons, thereby producing dysfunction of the motor nerves followed by Wallerian-like degeneration. In addition, it is controversial whether anti-GM1 antibodies interfere with motor axonal function and induce conduction failure
[
37
]
. Serologic evidence of
C. jejuni
infection in patients with GBS was correlated with anti-GM1b and anti-GalNAc-GD1a IgG antibodies
[
37
]
. The GD1a, GM1b, and GalNAc-GD1a epitopes are also present in
C. jejuni
LPSs isolated from patients with GBS
[
25
]
.
Molecular mimicry associated with CMV and
H. influenzae
As shown in Figure
2
, anti-GM2 IgM and IgG antibodies were found in patients who developed GBS subsequent to CMV infection
[
38
]
. GM2 was not detectable by standard immunohistochemical techniques in human peripheral nerve, although GM2 antisera could lyse neural membranes containing GM2
[
39
]
. These findings raise doubts about the pathophysiological significance of anti-GM2 IgM antibody subsequent to CMV infection
[
18
]
. An absorption study showed that CMV-infected fibroblasts express the GM2 epitope. Viruses do not encode glycosylating enzymes; therefore, CMV infection of human fibroblasts may trigger upregulation of GM2 in the cell membrane
[
40
]
. Hence, these findings support the hypothesis that anti-GM2 IgM antibodies are induced in acute CMV infection by molecular mimicry between GM2 and the antigens induced by CMV infection
[
25
]
.
Figure 2.
Immunopathogenesis of Guillain–Barré syndrome.
Mori
et al
reported that AMAN patients had serological evidence of
H. influenzae
infection and anti-GM1 IgG antibody. The GM1 epitope has been found on the LPS of
H. influenzae
isolated from a patient with AMAN
[
41
]
. This finding suggests that molecular mimicry between the bacterium and human nerve tissue functions in the development of GBS after
H. influenzae
infection, as it does in GBS after
C. jejuni
enteritis.
Clinical presentation
GBS typically has a variable clinical presentation. It presents with a sudden, severe onset of peripheral neuropathy with a common pattern of ascending from lower limbs to upper body. The progression hits a plateau within 4 weeks
[
42
]
. The plateau phase can last between 7 days and 6 months, often then progressing toward resolution of the symptoms. Most of the patients are able to walk properly during the whole course of the disease, showing mild symptoms. One of the hallmark features of GBS is symmetric progression
[
11
]
. The neuropathy associated with GBS can affect the sensory, motor, and autonomic nervous system, thereby affecting the nerve supply to the peripheries
[
43
]
. It is considered monophasic, and relapse is usually not common. If the course of duration lasts for more than 6 weeks, it is imperative to consider other diagnoses
[
44
]
. GBS is characterized by a pattern of progressive drooping weakness, pain, or tingling in peripheries, often more severe in hospitalized patients
[
3
]
. The skeletal muscles typically exhibit weak or absence of reflexes. Additionally, diminished tone of muscles is another prominent sign seen in most cases. Along with the skeletal system, gastrointestinal system is often seen affected with symptoms of constipation, urinary retention, and abdominal distention
[
36
]
. The sensory symptoms are often nonlength dependent; hence, some patients report altered sensation
[
3
]
. GBS can involve the cranial nerves, that is, vagus, hypoglossal, and glossopharyngeal. Involvement of the respiratory, facial, and eye muscles is reported as well. BFP is one of the complications seen when facial nerves are affected
[
45
]
. Meningism can also be one of the manifestations of GBS, following muscle weakness.
Additionally, cardiovascular abnormalities have also been reported in about two-thirds of the cases
[
46
]
. There are no definitive testing procedures for the diagnosis of GBS. It is mainly reliant on clinical findings.
The most recent guidelines were developed by the Brighton Collaboration GBS working group in 2011, aiming to have a worldwide common criterion for diagnosis. It is divided into several levels to simplify the diagnosis. There are a total of five levels, as shown in Table
2
[
47
]
:

Definition and characteristics of ACD
ACD is defined as an increased TP concentration with a normal TNCC in the CSF
[
48
]
. Quantitatively, ACD is an elevated CSF protein despite normal leukocyte count (<5/µL) and erythrocyte count (<50/µL).
The exact pathophysiology of ACD is not yet fully understood. Many peripheral and central nervous system illnesses have been linked to ACD. Numerous mechanisms specific to the disease have been postulated, such as (1) intrathecal production or liberation of proteins like myelin basic protein and IgG; (2) dysfunction of the blood–brain barrier in meningeal or parameningeal inflammation; (3) dysfunction of the blood–nerve barrier in neuropathy; (4) sequestration of CSF in spinal compression; or (5) decreased CSF flow
[
49
]
.
Elaborating the blood–nerve barrier breakdown, when inflammation or immune-mediated damage/weaken the blood–nerve barrier, increased blood–nerve barrier permeability at the level of the proximal nerve roots in diseases like GBS. This makes it possible for bigger molecules, such as albumin, to seep into the CSF from the bloodstream while impeding the easy passage of white blood cells
[
50
]
. Moreover, there might be enhanced production of protein in CSF. While not always resulting in an inflammatory response that would raise the WBC count, some disorders lead to an excess of protein being produced inside the central nervous system. This can happen through enhanced synthesis by the choroid plexus or other mechanisms. Additionally, reduced reabsorption of CSF, when factors prevent the CSF from being absorbed normally, the CSF may accumulate protein without producing more white blood cells. Occasionally, the blood-CSF barrier’s processes will permit albumin to get through while limiting cell migration, causing a separation between protein and cell numbers. The distinctive discovery of increased protein levels in the CSF without a corresponding rise in white blood cells – a sign of ACD – is a result of these events
[
51
]
.
Recent advances in understanding the protein profile in ACD associated with GBS have revealed many crucial developments. According to some research, this process may entail the intrathecal synthesis or liberation of proteins like IgG. ACD can cause a high IgG index, indicating increased immunoglobulin production within the central nervous system. Studies demonstrate that the increased protein in CSF typically ranges from 100 to 1000 mg/dL. This elevation rises in diagnostic sensitivity over time, reaching about 80% by 3–4 weeks into the disease course
[
52
]
.
A frequent misconception, however, is that ACD must always be present to confirm the diagnosis
[
53
]
, (Table
3
) as only 64% of patients with GBS have this feature. Elevated CSF protein levels are found in approximately 50% of patients in the first 3 days after the onset of weakness, which increases to 80% after the first week
[
54
]
Despite this, albuminocytological separation remains the sole consistent CSF biomarker associated with GBS immunopathogenesis. It should also be highlighted that while abnormal electrophysiological results and an elevated protein level in CSF are hallmarks of GBS, patients can show normal results in both tests, particularly early in the disease’s course
[
55
]
.

A study of CSF features in GBS discovered that the albumin quotient (Qalb) and TP levels in CSF have a strong link, and these markers can be markedly raised, especially as the time from symptom start to lumbar puncture (LP) increases. CSF protein levels rise despite low cell counts (<50 cells/µL), meeting GBS diagnostic criteria
[
55
]
.
Significance of ACD in GBS diagnosis
Patients with suspected GBS usually undergo a series of standard tests, including blood counts, glucose, electrolytes, kidney function, and liver enzymes. These tests help diagnose and manage the condition. Results of these tests can be used to exclude other causes of acute flaccid paralysis, such as infections or metabolic or electrolyte dysfunctions
[
56
]
. Typically, testing for preceding infections is not crucial for diagnosing GBS. However, it can offer valuable insights into the epidemiology of the disease during outbreaks of infectious diseases like Zika virus and
C. jejuni
infection
[
57
]
. The diagnostic value of measuring serum levels of antiganglioside antibodies is limited and assay-dependent. A positive test result can be helpful, especially when the diagnosis is in doubt, but a negative test result does not rule out GBS
[
58
]
.
Electrophysiological examination in patients with GBS will reveal a sensorimotor polyradiculoneuropathy or polyneuropathy, indicated by reduced conduction velocities, reduced sensory and motor evoked amplitudes, abnormal temporal dispersion, and partial motor conduction blocks. Typical for GBS is a “sural sparing pattern” in which the sural sensory nerve action potential is normal while the median and ulnar sensory nerve action potentials are abnormal or even absent
[
59
]
. Electrodiagnostic studies can help identify AIDP, AMAN, and AMSAN
[
60
]
. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is not usually used to diagnose GBS, but it can help rule out other conditions that might be causing the symptoms, such as brainstem infection, stroke, or spinal cord inflammation
[
56
]
. The clinical diagnosis of GBS needs to be confirmed by CSF analysis
[
43
]
.
Differential diagnosis
There are disorders that may mimic GBS like tick-paralysis, HIV, and West Nile Virus which have similar clinical manifestations
[
61
]
. Tick paralysis is induced by a neurotoxin in the tick’s salivary glands. GBS and tick-paralysis rarely present with fever or pain. Both may affect the cranial nerves, but GBS affects III, IV, VI, and VII. To distinguish them apart, pupillary dilation is seen with tick paralysis, and the CSF would show pleocytosis in West Nile Virus or HIV rather than ACD
[
62
]
. Similarly, an increased lymphocyte count would be inconsistent with GBS and may suggest sarcoidosis, Lyme disease neuropathy, or recent HIV infection
[
63
]
. All diseases that attack the spinal cord, peripheral nerves, muscles, neuromuscular junctions, and cerebral vessels may result in weakness, like GBS, and need to be considered in the differential diagnosis
[
64
]
. To make a formal diagnosis of GBS, two clinical criteria are required – progressive weakness in more than one limb and areflexia (or distal areflexia with proximal hyporeflexia).
ACD
, nerve conduction findings, disease progression over days to 4 weeks, symmetry, mild sensory abnormalities, cranial nerve involvement, autonomic dysfunction, and recovery that starts in 2 to 4 weeks all support a diagnosis of GBS
[
65
]
. The Various biomarkers of GBS and their clinical significance are mentioned in the Table
4
.

Recent advancements in GBS diagnosis
Biomarkers are objectively assessed characteristics that indicate physiological and pathological responses to therapeutic interventions
[
66
]
. While ACD remains a reliable CSF biomarker for GBS, other possible biomarkers should be investigated. Interleukin 8 (IL-8) has been discovered as a possible biomarker for differentiating GBS. Two cytokine screening-based investigations have demonstrated a trend of CSF IL-8 rise in patients with GBS
[
67
]
.
Plasma cytokine alterations in patients with GBS have also been documented, indicating that plasma biomarkers may play a role in understanding the immunological processes of GBS. Cytokines have a crucial role as both upstream and downstream mediators in numerous inflammatory disorders. In fact, numerous investigations have found that a complex cytokine system plays a role in the pathogenesis of GBS, either by increasing or inhibiting inflammation, or by acting in tandem. Pro-inflammatory cytokines, such as IFN-γ, TNF-α, and IL-6, -17, -22, and -23, have been linked to the development of GBS. TNF-α and IFN-γ levels were elevated during the acute phase of GBS, but reduced during the recovery period, indicating a potential link to GBS progression. Antiinflammatory cytokines such IL-4, IL-10, and TGF-β may reduce inflammation response, while IL-27 first pro-inflammatory and subsequently antiinflammatory following recovery in GBS
[
68
]
.
Keddie
et al
developed a very sensitive immunoassay to detect the intermediate filament protein peripherin in blood. A study showed that peak peripherin levels were higher in GBS than all other peripheral nervous system injuries
[
69
]
.
A study used high-sensitivity shotgun mass spectrometry to characterize the CSF lipidome of patients with GBS. The analysis of 222 CSF lipid molecular species indicated distinct differences in absolute and relative lipid contents in GBS. For the GBS group, the fourfold increase in total lipid content was a distinguishing and previously unknown hallmark of Peripheral Nervous System (PNS) demyelination. This highlights the utility of broad-range shotgun lipidomic analysis as a quick and dependable approach of biomarker discovery in patients with demyelinating neurological diseases such as GBS, which could be a beneficial diagnostic supplement to existing tests
[
70
]
.
Ganglioside autoantibodies target glycosphingolipids in the peripheral nervous system that contain sialic acid. Both IgG and IgM isotypes are linked to GBS antibodies against Diagnosis Related Group (DRG) neurons are much more common in patients with GBS. Serum antibodies to glycolipids, primarily gangliosides, are identified in approximately 60% of patients with GBS. These antibodies cause autoimmune targeting of peripheral nerve locations, resulting in neurological injury
[
71
]
. Several new technologies and biomarkers can assist in distinguishing between GBS subtypes. Some of the markers available for investigation include levels of soluble receptor for advanced glycation end products, an integrated metabolomic method using CSF samples, plasma lipid metabolites, cytokines, and T-cell ratios
[
66
]
.
Advanced neuroimaging techniques, such as those that evaluate cerebral blood flow, metabolism, white matter connections, and neural network activation, hold considerable promise in this field. Machine learning has also been utilized to quantify neurodegenerative patterns in structural MRI research. Spinal tap, electromyography, and nerve conduction investigations are some of the current diagnostic methods for GBS. A new potential diagnostic tool in GBS is ultrasound imaging of the peripheral nerves, which has revealed enlarged cervical nerve roots early in the disease course, indicating the importance of spinal root inflammation as an early pathological mechanism

72
]
.
Nerve conduction studies (NCS) can help to support the clinical diagnosis of GBS and discriminate between axonal and demyelinating subtypes. Diagnosis of GBS can sometimes be difficult in the early phase of the disease, especially when reflexes are still present or the weakness is not distributed according to the classic pattern (for instance, in patients with paraparesis). NCS can demonstrate abnormalities in locations with subclinical disease, such as the arms. NCS findings of peripheral neuropathy or polyradiculopathy can also help to confirm the diagnosis of GBS
[
73
]
.
Nerve conduction abnormalities tend to peak >2 weeks after the onset of weakness
[
74
]
. However, if NCS are required to confirm a diagnosis of suspected GBS, a delay of 2 weeks is often too long. Although NCS can be performed earlier in the disease course, the results might still be normal at this stage. Often, the first-detected NCS abnormalities are prolonged or absent F-waves, although other conduction abnormalities become evident as the disease progresses. To increase the diagnostic yield of NCS, at least four motor nerves, three sensory nerves, and F-waves should be investigated
[
73
]
. Since no consensus exists on which neurophysiological criteria are best for confirming the diagnosis of GBS subtype, multiple classification systems are used

Limitations
ACD in GBS refers to the separation of albumin levels in CSF and serum. This finding is used as a diagnostic criterion for GBS
[
75
]
.
ACD is also highly contingent on the timing of LP, with lower numbers early in the disease process. The frequency of ACD is reported to vary between 44% and 81%, depending on the timing of LP
[
76
]
.
Furthermore, ACD is not exclusive to GBS as it can present in other neurological conditions. ACD has been described in a large number of peripheral and central nervous system disorders. Several disease-specific mechanisms have been proposed, including (1) the intrathecal production or liberation of proteins such as IgG and myelin basic protein, (2) blood–brain barrier dysfunction in meningeal or parameningeal inflammation, (3) blood–nerve barrier dysfunction in neuropathy, (4) sequestration of CSF in spinal compression, or (5) decreased CSF flow

]

The proportion of the CSF that was used for analysis could have influenced CSF measurements since a previous study showed that protein concentrations decrease between the first (0th–4th) milliliters and the last (21st–24th) milliliters. Standard CSF collection practice at different institutions is to take approximately 10–12 mL of CSF partitioned into four to five sterile tubes, and analysis is usually carried out using one of the first three tubes

]
.
LP is an invasive procedure which can cause complications such as spinal hematoma and postdural puncture headache

Conclusion
GBS presents as a serious neurological condition that demands urgent medical attention, as it often develops rapidly following infections and involves the body’s immune system attacking its own nerves. One of its key diagnostic clues is the finding of elevated protein without corresponding white blood cells in spinal fluid (ACD), which helps doctors differentiate GBS from similar neurological disorders. While this spinal fluid pattern consistently supports the diagnosis, exactly why it occurs remains unclear, pointing to important gaps in our understanding of how GBS develops at a biological level. Ongoing research into these underlying mechanisms could not only solve this mystery but also help determine whether this spinal fluid change might predict disease severity or outcomes. Such knowledge would enable healthcare teams to identify cases earlier and initiate appropriate treatments more quickly. With exciting progress in protein analysis and biomarker technology, combining these modern tools with classic findings like the characteristic spinal fluid changes may lead to more tailored diagnostic and treatment strategies for patients battling this challenging condition.
